content: Chinese medicinal herbs are commonly utilized in China for the treatment of the common cold. However, their efficacy has not been systematically evaluated to date. The objective of this study was to determine the effectiveness and safety of Chinese medicinal herbs in managing the common cold. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), MEDLINE, EMBASE, AMED, the Chinese Biomedical Database (CBMdisc), and the China National Knowledge Infrastructure (CNKI). The search spanned from 1966 to May 2008, depending on the database. The inclusion criteria were randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that investigated the efficacy of Chinese medicinal herbs for treating the common cold. Four review authors contacted the original trial authors of the identified RCTs to confirm the randomization procedures. Data extraction and analysis were performed by two review authors for trials that met the inclusion criteria. A total of 17 studies involving 3,212 patients were identified. Among these, 15 studies were determined to have a high risk of bias, while only two studies were assessed as having a low risk of bias. The trials used positive drugs as controls, but the efficacy of these control drugs was not clearly established. Nearly all trials tested different Chinese herbal preparations, with only one trial testing the same herbal preparation twice. In seven trials, six herbal preparations demonstrated greater effectiveness in enhancing recovery compared to the control treatments. However, in the remaining 10 studies, seven herbal preparations did not show a statistically significant difference in efficacy when compared to the control treatments. One study failed to report the differences between the intervention and control groups. The authors concluded that Chinese herbal medicines may have the potential to shorten the symptomatic phase of the common cold. However, due to the lack of trials with a sufficiently low risk of bias, the absence of placebo-controlled studies, and the use of control drugs with unclear efficacy, there is insufficient evidence to recommend any specific Chinese medicinal herbs for the treatment of the common cold.
